e.t: Agag is a proper name, referring to a person named Agag in the Greek Old Testament. The word does not describe a general quality, action, or object; it identifies this individual by name. In this LXX corpus, it occurs eight times, all within five verses of 1 Samuel 15, from verses 8 through 33. The name is rendered consistently as “Agag.” Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity but does not by itself explain the person’s actions or significance in each occurrence.

This word is a proper name rendered “Adasa,” with “Athasa” also given as a form of the name. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears twice, both times in 1 Maccabees. The available references are 1 Maccabees 7:40 and 7:45, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the specific identity or role named in those passages cannot be stated safely.

This word means “sister,” referring to a female sibling. It is a noun used for a woman described in relation to another person as a sister. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs 105 times, showing that this is a regularly used family-relationship term rather than a rare expression. Its precise reference—whether to a particular woman or to a relationship named in a passage—comes from the surrounding sentence and context. The same meaning appears across books including Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Ezekiel.

Ainan, also rendered Enan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies people mentioned in genealogical, tribal, and census-related passages. The name occurs ten times across ten verses, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Nehemiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise reference is determined by the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains that of a personal name.

gl: in full bloom; at the prime
d: in full bloom; at the prime

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that is in full bloom or at the prime—the point of fullest development or vigor. It presents the subject as being at its best or most mature stage, rather than beginning, declining, or incomplete. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in 3 Maccabees 4:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a person or thing at the height of its condition.

This word means “flour,” the finely prepared grain product used in food preparation and offerings. It is a noun naming a tangible substance rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across 13 verses, including passages describing food prepared for visitors, household provision, and material brought in worship. Its ordinary sense remains straightforward: ground grain ready to be used in cooking or presented as part of an offering. The surrounding verse determines the specific use, but the word itself refers to flour.

“Amadathou” or “Amathathu” is a proper name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This Greek LXX name appears six times across five verses in Esther, from Esther 1:1 through Esther 9:24. Its precise identification and significance in any particular sentence depend on the surrounding verse, since the name itself functions primarily to identify an individual. The two forms preserved in the gloss reflect the name’s recorded renderings in this Greek Old Testament text.

This noun refers to an indication—something that points out or makes something known—or to an appointment, meaning an arranged designation or setting apart. Its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea concerns making something recognizable or assigning something for a particular purpose. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 43:6. This word should therefore be understood from its basic sense rather than treated as a broad recurring biblical term.

This LXX Greek verb means “have respite” or “give relief.” It describes either coming to a period of rest and refreshment or providing relief to someone else. The central idea is release from weariness, pressure, or trouble, according to how the sentence uses the verb. It occurs 64 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it can describe both receiving rest and bringing rest to others. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This LXX Greek verb means “hold close/onto; reach.” It describes taking hold of something, clinging to it, or extending toward it. As an action word, its exact sense depends on what a person is holding or reaching for in the sentence. It occurs 41 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Genesis, Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The word can therefore express either firm attachment or movement toward a goal, while retaining the central idea of grasping, maintaining contact, or reaching out.

gl: take off turban; take off tiara
d: take off turban; take off tiara

e.t: This verb means to take off a turban or tiara. It describes removing a head covering or ceremonial crown, rather than putting one on. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus, where the wording concerns distinctive headwear. The specific force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic action remains removal: taking the turban or tiara away. This is a concrete action word, not a general term for changing clothing or appearance.

This noun means “standing away from,” describing a position of separation, withdrawal, or distance from something. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in two passages of 2 Chronicles and one passage in Ezra. Its basic sense focuses on being apart rather than remaining with or attached to something. The surrounding verse determines what kind of separation is intended in each occurrence.

This adjective describes someone as weak-minded—lacking firmness or strength of mind. It identifies a person’s mental weakness rather than naming an action or object. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 15:5. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary sense remains a description of a person whose mind is not strong or steadfast.

This verb means “act foolishly,” describing behavior marked by poor judgment or a failure to act wisely. It presents foolish action rather than merely naming a foolish person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 10:21. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains the act of behaving foolishly. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entry.

This Greek LXX noun means “depth,” referring to the deep part or extent of something. It can describe physical depths, such as the depths of the earth or sea, and can also express profound distance or immeasurable reach. The word appears 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages from Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on whether the surrounding passage speaks of a physical location, great distance, or figurative profundity.

Bakchir is a proper name, also given as “Vakkhir.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 34:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic meaning is the personal name Bakchir or Vakkhir.

Bariga, also rendered Variga, is a proper name rather than a descriptive word. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text and does not itself express an action, quality, or relationship. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 8:16. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone gives no further meaning beyond identifying the individual it names.

This LXX word is a proper name, rendered “Beriga” or “Veriga.” It functions as a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in 1 Chronicles. Because no further definition or verse text is provided, its meaning is chiefly its role as the name of a named person in those genealogical records.

This noun means “mortal man”: a human being understood as subject to death and human limitation. It identifies people in contrast with what is not mortal, emphasizing the ordinary condition of human life rather than describing a particular person’s character. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, all within Job, where it is used in statements about humanity. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “tongue,” the bodily organ in the mouth. It can refer to the tongue itself as a physical part of the body, and its normal use may connect with what the tongue does in speaking or expressing words. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 148 times, showing that this is a regularly used word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective means “speckled,” describing something marked with small spots or distinct patches of color. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for the appearance of animals in the account of Jacob’s flocks. The word occurs eight times across seven verses, all in Genesis 30–31, so its scriptural use is focused on visible coloring or markings rather than an abstract quality. It describes an outward pattern that distinguishes one animal from another.

This verb means “fight through”: to struggle onward against opposition rather than simply remain passive. It expresses active engagement in a difficult contest or resistance. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times—four in Sirach and once in Daniel—showing a focused but recurring use for determined struggle. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains pressing through conflict by fighting.

This noun means “tearing in pieces”—the act of being pulled or ripped apart. It describes a violent separation rather than a mild division. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 15:3. The word itself identifies the kind of action being described, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that action functions in its sentence. Its central idea remains the forceful breaking apart of something into pieces.

This Greek LXX verb means “divide the hoof.” It describes the physical feature used in Israel’s dietary instructions to distinguish animals by their split hooves. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14, where animals are examined according to this characteristic. It names an observable condition rather than expressing an action of moral or spiritual division. As a verb, it describes what an animal’s hoof does or is characterized by: being divided into separate parts.

This LXX verb means “hold power”—to exercise authority or control over others. It describes someone who possesses governing strength or influence, rather than merely having ability in the abstract. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on who is exercising power and over whom, but its central idea remains the possession or use of authority.

This verb means to enter or go in—to move from outside to inside, or to come into a place or situation. It describes physical movement in the Greek Old Testament, and its ordinary force is straightforward: someone or something crosses into a location. The word occurs 624 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a common term for entering. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what person, place, or setting the surrounding passage identifies.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “lend at interest,” describing the act of providing money as a loan while requiring interest in return. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 22:24 and Deuteronomy 23:20. Its precise force in either passage is determined by the surrounding verse and larger command, but its basic meaning remains the action of lending money for interest.

This Greek LXX verb means to fly out—to move outward through the air or leave by flying. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so its exact force depends on what is flying and the surrounding sentence. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 43:14. Its basic sense is straightforward: something takes flight and goes out from its place. No broader related theme or specialized meaning is established here.

This Greek LXX verb means “cast forth”: to throw or send something outward from its present place. As a verb, it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Psalm 1:4. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but the word itself centers on something being cast out or driven away.

This verb means “diminish”: to become less, or to make something less. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes reduction in quantity or extent rather than increase. It occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, with uses spanning Genesis, Exodus, Kings, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is becoming smaller or being reduced there.

This adjective describes something that is curved or twisted rather than straight. It refers to a bent, winding shape or form. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus 6:14 and 1 Kings 6:8. Its exact force in either passage depends on the object being described and the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a shape that bends, turns, or follows a winding course. It is therefore a physical description, not a statement about character, belief, or moral condition.

This Greek LXX verb means to hope—to look toward something expected or desired with confidence. It expresses an active posture of relying on a hoped-for outcome, rather than merely naming a vague wish. In the Septuagint, it occurs 105 times, almost entirely in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures, with especially frequent use in the Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the speaker is hoping in, but the central idea remains confident expectation directed toward a future good or deliverance.

This noun means “continuity” or “persistency”: something continuing steadily and not stopping. It describes ongoing persistence rather than a brief or isolated act. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, chiefly in passages from Exodus, Numbers, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Sirach. Its meaning remains focused on sustained continuance, while the surrounding passage determines what is continuing and why. As an LXX word, it belongs to the Greek rendering tradition of the Old Testament and should be understood within that corpus.

gl: thing to take pleasure in; delight
d: thing to take pleasure in; delight

e.t: This noun refers to a “thing to take pleasure in; delight”—something enjoyed or valued because it brings pleasure. It describes an object of enjoyment rather than an action or command. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 2:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains something regarded as a source of pleasure or delight.

This Greek LXX verb means “put out flowers,” describing the act of producing or displaying blossoms. It is a word of flowering or coming into bloom, rather than a name for the flower itself. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, Isaiah, Hosea, and Song of Songs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the appearance or production of flowers.

This Greek LXX verb means “come to aid” or “help.” It describes the action of assisting someone, especially by coming to their support. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 13:17. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the context. Its basic sense remains an active response that provides help or support.

This adjective describes something as “in danger” or “dangerous.” It can identify a person, situation, or circumstance exposed to harm or capable of causing harm. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:33, so its normal meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that verse depends on what the adjective describes.

This word means “seventeenth,” identifying someone or something as number 17 in an ordered sequence. As an adjective, it describes a person, object, or time connected with that position rather than naming the thing itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears four times, including passages in Kings and Chronicles. Its basic meaning remains an ordinal marker; the surrounding verse determines what person, object, or time is being numbered.

This Greek LXX verb means “find”: to discover, locate, or come upon someone or something. It describes the act of finding rather than merely looking, and its precise sense is shaped by what is being sought and the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 528 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a common verb for expressing discovery or finding in many kinds of situations.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something that gives off a pleasant, sweet fragrance. It refers to a pleasing smell rather than to taste, appearance, or character. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including two occurrences in Exodus and two in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains “sweet-smelling” or “fragrant”; the surrounding verse determines what particular object or substance is being described.

Zambram, also rendered Zamvram, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 46:13. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person; the name itself is not presented here with an additional definition or description. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This verb means to inspect the liver for soothsaying—that is, to seek an omen or prediction by examining an animal’s liver. It describes a specific divinatory practice rather than ordinary medical examination. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Ezekiel 21:26. The surrounding verse is needed to explain its particular force there, but the word itself plainly identifies liver inspection as a means of seeking supernatural guidance.

In the Greek Old Testament, this noun refers to “idols.” It names things regarded as objects of worship, rather than describing an action or quality. This LXX word occurs twice, in Judges 17:5 and 2 Chronicles 35:19, so its recorded use is limited. Its central meaning remains straightforward: idols in the Old Testament setting. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use in either passage.

This noun refers to teraphim—idols associated with forbidden worship rather than the worship of the living God. It can be rendered “idols,” while “teraphim” preserves the traditional name for these objects. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in five Old Testament verses: three in Judges, one in 1 Samuel, and one in 2 Kings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is an idol or household image used in false worship.

gl: part of the temple; I saw
d: part of the temple; I saw

e.t: This rare Greek LXX noun refers to a part of the temple. Its recorded meaning also includes “I saw,” though that phrase does not fit the noun’s ordinary grammatical function as clearly as the temple-related sense. It occurs only once in the Greek LXX, at Ezekiel 41:8. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise role there cannot be explained further; its clearest standalone meaning is a temple-related part or section.

This noun means “byword”: a person or thing spoken of as a familiar public example. It describes something reduced to a commonly repeated saying or expression, rather than naming an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job, at Job 17:6 and Job 30:9. The surrounding verse determines what person or thing is being called a byword in each passage. This word is a proper name rendered “Iasoubi” or “Iasuvi,” identifying a named individual in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the Greek Septuagint, at Numbers 26:20, but the verse text is not available here, so its broader role in that passage cannot be described from the name alone. As a name, it functions primarily to identify the individual rather than express an action, quality, or general idea.

Iedlaph is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It is identified by the forms “Iedlaph” and “Iethlaf,” which represent the same named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Genesis 22:22. The name itself does not provide a broader general meaning; its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

This Greek LXX verb refers to a horseman, a person who rides or acts on horseback. It presents the idea in verbal form rather than simply naming a person or animal. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 9:16, Ezekiel 23:23, and Micah 1:13. These occurrences show its use across several Old Testament books, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise role in any one passage.

This word is a proper name rendered “Kabsaim” or “Kavsem.” It identifies a named place or location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 21:22. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points readers to the specific location named in that passage, while the surrounding verse supplies its historical and geographical significance.

Kalamō, also rendered Kalamo, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a specific person, place, or thing named in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament, all within Ezekiel, across nine verses from Ezekiel 40:5 through 42:19. Its precise identity and significance therefore depend on the surrounding passage, not on the name alone.

This Greek LXX verb means “apprehend”: it describes taking hold of or capturing someone or something. It is an action word, so it tells what a person does rather than naming an object or quality. The word occurs 115 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is used broadly across these writings. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This verb means “besmear with”: to spread or coat something over a surface. It describes an action in which one substance is applied to another, rather than merely touching or being near it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times, including once in Exodus and twice in Wisdom. The exact object being coated must be understood from the surrounding verse, but the word itself centers on applying something over or onto another thing.

This verb means being drunk: being under the influence of too much alcohol. It describes a person’s condition rather than an object or place, and its basic sense is physical intoxication. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Habakkuk 2:5. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its particular force there, but the word itself directly expresses drunkenness. This LXX word should be understood as a Greek rendering in the Old Testament corpus, distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

This Greek LXX verb means “let loose” or “untie.” It describes releasing someone or something from restraint, fastening, or confinement. The same basic action can be expressed when a person is freed, an animal is released, or something tied is undone. It occurs 24 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its meaning is established across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being released or untied.

“Midwife” means a person who assists a mother during childbirth. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun names the person who helps women give birth, rather than describing the child, mother, or birth itself. It occurs nine times in eight verses across Genesis and Exodus, with most occurrences in Exodus. Its precise force in any individual sentence comes from that passage’s surrounding wording.

This word means “testimony”. It refers to evidence or a statement that serves to establish what is true. As a noun, it can describe the testimony itself rather than the person giving it. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly, appearing 220 times from Genesis through Sirach. Its central idea remains a witness-bearing declaration or proof, whether connected with people, events, or sacred matters. The surrounding passage determines the precise kind of testimony intended.

This proper name refers to Memphis, also called Memfis, an Egyptian city. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The name occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament, across Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Hosea. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and its treatment of Memphis, but the word itself simply names the city. It appears in Isaiah 19:13, Jeremiah 2:16 and 26:14, 26:19, and Ezekiel 30:13 and 30:15.

This word refers to “tainting” or “defilement.” It is a noun that names the condition or result associated with something being tainted or defiled, rather than describing the action as a verb. Its meaning remains focused on moral or ritual pollution in the broad sense of defilement. In the LXX corpus, it occurs twice, showing that it is an uncommon noun used in specific passages rather than a frequently repeated term. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding text.

This Greek LXX adjective means “myriad,” referring to a very large number or multitude. It describes something counted in an amount so great that the emphasis falls on abundance rather than a small, exact total. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, including passages in Judges, Chronicles, Esther, Job, and the Maccabean books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense consistently points to a vast quantity.

Nasarach is a proper name, referring to a person named Nasarach, also rendered Nasarakh. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Isaiah 37:38. The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not include the verse text or surrounding context, so it does not establish additional meaning beyond the person’s name. Its precise significance in that verse must be understood from the passage itself.

This noun means “young man,” referring to a male who is youthful or in the younger stage of life. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it is used 84 times, including descriptions of young men in ordinary human settings. The word identifies age and sex, but the surrounding passage determines what the young man is doing or why he is mentioned. Its basic sense remains focused on a youthful male person.

This word means “carbonate of soda,” a mineral substance named in the Greek Old Testament. It is a noun, so it identifies a material rather than an action, quality, or person. In the LXX, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 2:22. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the word’s precise use in that verse must be understood from its context. Its basic lexical meaning remains clear: carbonate of soda.

This word means “night,” the period of darkness between evening and morning. It is a noun used for the nighttime itself and for events or actions associated with that part of the day. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 244 times, showing that it is a normal, broadly used word for marking time. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its basic meaning remains the dark portion of the daily cycle.

Ozias is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies someone by name. This name occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing especially in 2 Chronicles, and also in 1 Chronicles, 2 Kings, and Isaiah. The name is rendered “Ozias” in the available English translation support. Its exact role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function remains personal identification.

“Home-born” describes someone born within a household rather than brought in from outside. It is an adjective used for people whose origin is connected with the household where they live or serve. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs 10 times, including passages in Genesis, Leviticus, Ecclesiastes, and Jeremiah. Its basic focus is birth or belonging within the household, while the surrounding verse determines the person’s particular role or situation.

This verb means “seated beside,” describing someone positioned next to another person. It presents sitting alongside someone as the central action, rather than naming the person or place involved. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Esther and Jeremiah. The surrounding verse determines who is seated beside whom and why that position matters in the passage. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to be seated next to someone.

This word means “well” or “fountain,” referring to a place or source where water is found. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for both natural springs and constructed wells. The word occurs 88 times in this LXX corpus, including descriptions of water sources and named locations. Its central idea is a dependable source of water, whether flowing naturally from the ground or gathered in a well.

This verb means to blow or sting. It describes an action that causes a painful strike or sharp hurt, whether the emphasis falls on the act of hitting or on the sensation produced. It appears once in this Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, at 2 Chronicles 29:9. Its exact force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea remains a blow or sting.

This word means “city.” It is a noun used for an inhabited place or community, whether the passage speaks of one city or more than one. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used widely—1,416 times—so it can refer to cities as a normal part of biblical geography and public life. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a water-hen, a water bird named in the Greek Old Testament. It is a noun used for a particular bird rather than for an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament: once in Leviticus 11:18 and once in Deuteronomy 14:18. Both references belong to the biblical lists of animals, so the word identifies the bird being mentioned there. Its exact significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the full list in which it appears.

This noun refers to an amulet or charm—an object associated with protection or special power. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in the Epistle of Jeremiah 1:69. The word itself identifies the kind of object being mentioned, while the surrounding verse is needed to understand how that object is regarded or used there. Its basic meaning remains an amulet or charm, rather than a person, action, or quality.

This verb means “protect” or “preside”: it describes taking responsibility for the care, direction, or oversight of others. Its basic sense includes standing in a position of active guardianship or leadership rather than merely being present. In the LXX, it occurs eight times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, showing use in several settings while retaining this central idea. The surrounding passage determines whether protection or presiding is most prominent in a particular verse.

This Greek LXX adverb means “first” or “foremost,” pointing to what comes before others in order or priority. It can describe the first action in a sequence or identify something as having the leading place. The word appears 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, including places translated “first.” Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains precedence—being first in time, order, or importance.

This word means “nose,” the part of the face used for breathing and smelling. It is a noun referring to the physical nose, whether speaking of a person or an animal. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 10 verses, including passages in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and other books. Its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: a bodily feature, with the surrounding verse determining whether the reference is human or animal. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, not a Greek New Testament entry.

This Greek LXX noun means “bodily strength” or “strength”—the physical power or vigor a person possesses. It names strength as a quality or capacity, rather than describing an action. In this LXX corpus, it occurs 15 times, with most occurrences in 1 Maccabees and one in Proverbs. The word therefore commonly refers to tangible human power or ability, while the surrounding sentence determines how that strength is being considered. Its stated lexical sense is consistent with the ordinary rendering “strength.”

Sabeu, also rendered Savev, is a proper name referring to a person named in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at Genesis 10:28. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not provide a broader definition or description, its meaning is best understood as this person’s name rather than as a general word describing an action, quality, or object.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named “Saleph,” also rendered “Salef.” It is not a description of an action, quality, or object, but identifies an individual by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 10:26. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is the personal name itself.

Samou, also rendered Samu, is a personal name. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:23.
